Affect as a Sign System

David Olds MD

David Olds

108 East 96th Street, 6F, New York, NY 10128, U.S.A
(email: ddolds@email.msn.com)

David Olds   Training and Supervising Analyst, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons, U.S.A.

This paper explores the idea that affects make up a semiotic system. After briefly presenting a version of modern semiotic theory—that of C. S. Pierce—the paper describes affects as sign systems of biological evaluation. Each of the major affects has a kind of vertical structure from brainstem to cortex and represents an analog evaluator in terms of one of the vectors important to survival. Each affect is a semiotic system in which there is a physiological bodily response, a display via the face and body, and a subjective awareness. The entire package leads to dispositions to approach or avoid and to have other evaluative subjective feelings. In nonhuman species, affects are represented by nonsymbolic signs. Humans have, in addition to the nonsymbolic, the symbolic capacity to name and speak about affects. The paper explores the advantages and possible functions of this capacity with respect to being aware of affects and finding evolutionary advantage in this awareness. Looking at this subject from the semiotic point of view allows us to shed light on: (1) the issue of the time course of an affect; (2) the concepts of drives and affects; (3) the three manifestations of affect and their dissociation; and (4) the different functions of the three types of signs with respect to affect.

Editors' Introduction

Edward Nersessian , Mark Solms , Oliver Turnbull and Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell  

This issue, 2003:1, arrives shortly after the joint publication of 2002:1 and 2002:2 and means that the Journal is now returned to being published on schedule.

The Target Article, by Edward Khantzian, focuses on addiction—a matter that has always been of great interest to psychoanalysis and has recently been at the center of substantial developments within neuroscience. Addiction is, of course, also a problem that is gaining increasing importance within modern industralized society. As readers will see, the Target Article has led to a lively set of commentaries—which have been responded to by Khantzian.

The four Original Articles in this issue cover some of the key concepts—in particular, affect and trauma—that form part of the common ground between psychoanalysis and the neurosciences. We also pleased to publish the Affective Neuroscience Personality Scales, which should bring the topic of quantitative personality research (and the currently dominant “Big Five” model) a much-needed reassessment in the context of neuroscience.

Also, as ever, this issue includes the usual departments of Book Reviews, Research Digest, and Bulletin.

We welcome the Journal back onto its appropriate schedule and offer advance warning that the 2003:2 issue will be published toward the end of this year.

Commentary on “Understanding Addictive Vulnerability”

George Koob PHD

George Koob

George Koob   The Scripps Research Institute, La Jolla, Calif., U.S.A.

The Neurobiology of Self-Regulation Failure in Addiction: An Allostatic View

Dr. Khantzian provides a cogent and scholarly argument for a psychodynamic view of addiction with a focus on what factors lead to the vulnerability for addiction. He identifies two critical elements (disordered emotions and disordered self-care) and two contributory elements (disordered self-esteem and disordered relationships). He further argues strongly for a modern self-medication hypothesis where individuals with substance-use disorders are hypothesized to take drugs as a “means to cope with painful and threatening emotions.” Khantzian makes the case that addicted individuals experience states of subjective distress and suffering that may or may not be associated with conditions meeting DSM-IV criteria for a psychiatric diagnosis (American Psychiatric Association, 1994) and consist mainly of feelings that are overwhelming and unbearable, but also may consist of an affective life that is absent and nameless.

Drug addiction is viewed as an attempt to medicate such a negative affective state, and Khantzian marshals significant psychodynamic evidence not only for the negative affective state, but also for the self-medication hypothesis. In addition, he argues that self-medication may be drug-specific, in that patients may have a preferential use of drugs that fits with the nature of the painful feeling states that they are self-medicating (e.g., opiates to counter intense anger and rage, stimulants as augmenting agents for high-energy individuals, energizing agents for low-energy individuals, and depressants for individuals who are tense and anxious). The common element argued by Khantzian is that each class of drugs serves as antidotes or correctives to dysphoric states and acts as a “replacement for a defect in the psychological structure” (Kohut, 1971) of such individuals.

Khantzian further argues that disordered self-care combines malignantly with the disordered emotional life to become the principal determinant of SUDs. Self-care deficits reflect an inability to ensure one's self-preservation and are characterized by an inability to anticipate or avoid harmful and dangerous situations and an inability to use appropriate judgment and feelings as guides in the face of danger. In other words, self-care deficits reflect an inability to appropriately experience emotions and appreciate the consequences of dangerous behaviors. Thus, the core element of his psychodynamic perspective is a dysregulated emotional system, or systems, in individuals vulnerable to addiction, and a dysregulation in how the emotions are expressed, experienced, and corrected.

Emotion, Placebo, and Ethics in Neuroscience

Oliver Turnbull PHD

Oliver Turnbull

Bangor, LL57 2DG, U.K.
(email: o.turnbull@bangor.ac.uk)

Oliver Turnbull   University of Wales, Bangor, U.K.

Featured Articles

Anderson, A. K., & Phelps, E. A. (2002). Is the human amygdala critical for the subjective experience of emotion? Evidence of intact dispositional affect in patients with amygdala lesions.Journal of Cognitive Neuro science, 14: 709-720.

Zald, D. H. (2003). The human amygdala and the emotional evaluation of sensory stimuli.Brain Research Reviews, 41: 88-123

If there is one brain region that has been promoted as the “centre” for emotion in recent years, it is the amygdala. This focus has been primarily because of a comprehensive series of findings begun from the work of LeDoux, and it has led to something of a reification of this brain structure. LeDoux (1996) himself has always been careful to point out that his work focuses only on one emotion (fear) and, indeed, only one aspect of fear (its memorial role in fear conditioning), but this appears not to have stopped others from assuming that the amygdala is where emotion happens. The regular activation of the amygdala in functional imaging investigations of emotion has confirmed this view. There have been others (notably Panksepp, 1998) who have pointed out that there is a range of other brain regions that appear to be engaged in emotion, that fear does not rely only on the amygdala, and, indeed, that electrical stimulation of many other brain areas produces even more intense fearful responses. Perhaps, it has been argued, the amygdala is involved only in the memorial aspects of fear, and other subcortical structures are central for the subjective experience of fear. However, this conclusion has been derived largely from work on animals and has awaited the systematic evaluation of subjective experience in humans. Because investigating subjective affective states remains (strangely enough) of low priority for many emotion researchers, we have waited for some time for a clear answer: this is now offered by the Anderson & Phelps and the Zald papers. Their data show that patients with amygdala damage—left, right, and bilateral—continue to experience subjective feelings of fear on a range of measures. It has taken emotion researchers a long time to do the first thing that a science of subjective experience (such as psychoanalysis) might have done on day one: ask the patient how he/she feels. Nevertheless, it is now clear that “the complexity and richness of human emotional life do not appear to be supported by the amygdala alone” (Anderson & Phelps, p. 717), and that “the human amygdala is neither necessary to consciously evaluate and report subjective emotional experiences, nor is it necessary for the more general subjective experience of affective states” (Zald, p. 113). There are many other brain regions that are known to play a role in emotional states, but we have yet to question what their precise role is in affective experience. We can now start the long process of establishing exactly what their contribution might be.

Editors' Introduction

Edward Nersessian , Mark Solms , Oliver Turnbull and Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell  

This issue (2003:2) arrives shortly after the publication of the 2002:1, 2002:2, and 2003:1 issues. It keeps our Journal on the publishing schedule that we wish to maintain: at the middle and end of each year.

The Target Article, by Vesa Talvitie and Juhani Ihanus, addresses and directly confronts John Searles critique of Freuds ideas about unconscious mental processes. The paper is followed by a set of commentaries that have in turn been responded to by Talvitie and Ihanus.

This issue also contains four Original Articles, three of which focus on the false-belief states of confabulation and dreaming. The final articlea remarkable piece of detective workfocuses on a fascinating issue in the history of neuro-psychoanalysis: the authorship of a dictionary article on aphasia, assumed to have been written by Freud and predating his 1891 book On Aphasia, that has long been considered influential in the early development of psychoanalysis.

Readers may also be interested to note that in this issue we have an extended, and timely, Book Review section. The section is entirely dedicated to Antonio Damasios latest book, Looking for Spinoza, in which Damasio fleshes out the philosophical underpinnings of his ideas on emotion and the body. The book is reviewed from a neuroscience perspective by Jaak Panksepp and Douglas Watt, and also by a Spinoza scholar, Heidi Ravven. Having dedicated her professional career to Spinozas work, Ravven informs us that the discovery of scientific data that appeared to confirm . . . the account of the emotions upon which Spinoza based his theory of ethics was like finding the Holy Grail (p. 219). This charming episode suggests that interdisciplinary epiphany can be experienced as much by neuro-philosophy as by neuro-psychoanalysis. We are pleased to be able to publish Damasios responses to both reviews

As ever, the 2003:2 issue ends with the usual departments of Research Digest and International Bulletin. In the Bulletin, Iréne Matthis welcomes reports from three new neuro-psychoanalysis groups (in Finland, Mexico, and the Northwestern states of the United States). By her count we now have more than 25 neuro-psychoanalysis groupsa trend that surely bodes well for our future.

On the Nature of Repressed Contents

A Working-Through of John Searle's Critique

Vesa Talvitie Lic. Psych. and Juhani Ihanus PHD

Juhani Ihanus

P.O. Box 9, FIN-00014 University of Helsinki, Finland
email: vesa.talvitie@helsinki.fi

Juhani Ihanus   Adjunct Professor of Cultural Psychology, University of Helsinki; Adjunct Professor of the History of Science and Ideas, University of Oulu; Lecturer, Open University of the University of Helsinki, Finland.

The philosopher John Searle has called Freud's idea about repressed contents “incoherent,” “factually empty,” and “implying dualism.” Thus he has been seen as a critic of psychoanalysis. This view is questioned in the present article. Searle shares the central ideas of psychoanalysis, and the differences between him and Freud are conceptual. Problems with unconscious meanings and mental contents of the repressed are treated here as philosophical, and the debate on this issue is suggested to have minor relevance for clinical data and psychoanalytic practice. The authors of this article prefer the terms “unconscious meaning preservation” and “meaning manipulation” instead of repressed contents. It is problematic to show how repressed contents would exist other than as neurophysiological structures. However, talk about repressed desires and memories is assessed as unavoidable and reasonable for psychoanalytic practice.

Commentary on “On the Nature of Repressed Contents”

Linda Brakel MD

Linda Brakel

Farmington Hills, Mich., U.S.A.

Linda Brakel  

I am very glad to have the opportunity to provide a commentary of Vesa Talvitie and Juhani Ihanus's [T & I's] target paper, “On the Nature of Repressed Contents—A Working-through of John Searle's Critique.” Although, as will be made evident, I disagree with T & I and with Searle, T & I have brought to the fore the vital issue of unconscious (representational) contents. This commentary is divided into three parts. First, I discuss T & I's attempt to reconcile Searle's critique of unconscious content with psychoanalysis. Second, I address problems with Searle's account of the ontology of the mental and his consequent critique of the psychoanalytic view of unconscious mental contents. Third, I attempt a positive argument in favor of unconscious (representational) contents.

Disagreement with T & I

T & I quote Searle (1992) in The Rediscovery of the Mind1 claiming that “the psychoanalytic idea of repressed contents … [is] ‘incoherent’ (p. 151), ‘factually empty’ (p. 167), and ‘implying dualism’ (p. 170).” Yet T & I hold that because the debate on this issue has but “minor relevance for clinical data and psychoanalytic practice,” a working-through could be facilitated by substituting T & I's terms “meaning preservation” and “meaning manipulation” for repressed unconscious contents. I disagree with the authors here.

1All Searle quotes are from The Rediscovery of the Mind (1992) unless otherwise specified.142

Commentary on “On the Nature of Repressed Contents”

Joel Weinberger

Joel Weinberger

Garden City, New York, U.S.A.

Joel Weinberger  

This is a topic well worth exploring. Searle is one of the preeminent philosophers wrestling with the problem of consciousness in the world today. Searle clearly believes in the power of unconscious processes (see Chapter 7 of The Rediscovery of the Mind, 1992): “The explanatory power of the notion of the unconscious is so great that we cannot do without it …” (p. 151). He believes however that the “Freudian conception of the relation between consciousness and the unconscious … is incoherent” (p. 151). As Freud is the preeminent theorist of the unconscious, this dispute is well worth exploring. If it could be resolved, this would be a major contribution to the study of the mind. Talvitie and Ihanus's notion that the conflict is more apparent than real—a consequence of choice of metaphors— is an intriguing one. Their solution involving the creation of a third set of terms to solve the dilemma (e.g., unconscious meaning preservation for repressed meanings) is worth exploring.

Before I go further, however, there seems to be confusion in their article that makes it very difficult for me to judge its points. The authors seem to equate repression with unconscious. Thus they assert that: “The basic logic behind the term repression is that to be conscious of a content is distinct from its efficacy—a content does not have to be conscious to affect behavior.” And again: “According to the terminology introduced above, repressed contents involve representations that have no direct consequences for the contents of consciousness.” This definition can hold for any unconscious process or content. It does not capture the unique properties of a repressed content. A cognitive scientist and/or a social psychologist would be perfectly comfortable with it as a description of what they would term implicit processes. It could describe an automatic process, perceptual fluency, implicit memory, or a multitude of other processes studied by cognitive theorists and researchers. For a content to be repressed, it must arouse anxiety that then motivates the person to keep it from reaching consciousness. It then must continually strive for expression. This then leads to all of the vicissitudes of the unconscious that are so unique to psychoanalytic theory. Searle has no problem with repression defined in this way. “And no doubt there are many [mental states] that could not be brought to consciousness for one reason or another—they may be too painful and hence too deeply repressed for us to think about them, for example” (p. 154). So what are the authors interested in reconciling? It is certainly not the conception of repression. Furthermore, what is repression? These conceptual and terminological confusions need to be cleared up before I can feel comfortable in offering a sensible critique of their article.

Irith Raveh

Irith Raveh

Irith Raveh  

The forum was established in September 2000 by and for professionals from different disciplines within the human service professions. It is comprised of persons interested in designing and operating a permanent forum of learning on the interrelationship between psychoanalysis and brain and behavioral sciences. The intent is to study the emotional, mental, physical, and bioneurological components from both perspectives, fully keeping in mind the uniqueness of each. The desired yield of this enterprise is the creation of a common language for discourse and thus better comprehension of the interrelationship between the two, and the promotion of further investigation of neuropsychoanalytical issues. The assumption is that this will pave the way for advancements in the science of human behavior and will improve the lives of people, thus contributing to advancing humanity within society, in line with the mission of these professions.

The group consists of approximately 15 members who attend monthly evening meetings (alternating between Tel-Aviv and Jerusalem) as well as more extended meetings, where participants are expected to present lectures on a topic related to the annual program.

This year the subject was issues of the self viewed from a psychoanalytic and a neurological context. We examined the concepts “self” and “agency” from our various points of view, striving to define their primary core modules. We completed a list of primitives (elementary building blocks) of the concepts. We will continue our work using research material, and we hope to be able to present the result at next year's scientific meeting.

At the same time we have been discussing a procedure of scientific research called “the cave—virtual reality,” where we try to compare the differences and the similarities to the concept of transference/counter-transference, using aspects from both neurology and psychoanalysis.

Report from the Fourth International Neuro-Psychoanalysis Congress, New York, 25-28 July 2003

Lennart Ramberg MD

Lennart Ramberg

Lennart Ramberg   Member of the Swedish Psychoanalytical Association, a Provisional Society in the IPA

As a result of SARS outbreak in Toronto, this year's Congress, on “The Unconscious in Cognitive Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis,” was swiftly relocated to New York. In spite of the many problems this must have caused, the conference was particularly smoothly organized.

At the well-attended journal launch hosted by Other Press, I was pleased to finally hold in my hands the double issue of Volume 4 and the first issue of Volume 5 of Neuro-Psychoanalysis (now published by Karnac Books). I am sure we all look forward to a more regularly published journal!

I am glad I decided to attend the optional Education Day held the day before the Congress, because this initiative was a true pedagogic success. Maggie Zellner's overview of brain anatomy and neurophysiology provided a perfect starting point. The comprehensive notes she provided allowed us to really concentrate on the lectures. Oliver Turnbull described the basic circuits of emotion and motivation (see Neuro-Psychoanalysis, 1, No. 1, for more on this). Yoram Yovell enlightened us about new ways of understanding the role of memory in trauma (see also Neuro-Psychoanalysis, 2, No. 2). Dr. Yovell also used his research to illustrate new insights on how flashbulb memories are built up. Finally, Mark Solms provided a neuro-psychoanalytic overview of Freud's structural model.

The main conference began with Drew Westen's talk on “Unconscious Conflict and Compromise; Affect Regulation and Connectionist Networks.” Westen held true to the integrative aim of neuro-psychoanalysis by illustrating the advantages and disadvantages of the concepts of the unconscious held by psychoanalysis and cognitive science. Howard Shevrin's counterpoint offered examples of research that uses subliminal processes to scientifically test the Unconscious.

Mark Solms then demonstrated that the prefrontal cortex can be looked upon as the neuroanatomical matrix for the ego. Solms explained that the pleasure principle actually represses what the primitive, archaic ego cannot tolerate. Solms also used clinical examples from his work with Korsakoff's syndrome to suggest what psychoanalytic knowledge can bring to neuroscience. In his counterpoint, the neuroscientist Todd Feinberg came to conclusions similar to those of Solms. Feinberg described the way many of his patients also showed a disowned insight into their predicament. He conveyed their existential situation through the anxiety-filled reports from an imaginary adopted child. Marcel Kinsbourne's (neuroscientific) counterpoint was not outspoken. He pointed out that when the brain's work is not constrained as in (ideal) free association, it starts to symbolize.

How Dreams and Memory May Be Related

Eugen Tarnow PHD

Eugen Tarnow

18-11 Radburn Road, Fair Lawn, NJ 07410, U.S.A

Eugen Tarnow   Avalon Business Systems, Inc., Riverdale, New York, U.S.A.

This paper presents a theory of dreams and long-term memory structure that proposes that both entities are closely related. The theory is based on a variation of Freud's dream theory: (1) Freud's “unconscious” is relabeled the “long-term memory structure” (LTMS); (2) it is proposed that dreams are ever-present excitational responses to perturbations of perceptions and thought, during waking life as well as sleep, which only become conscious when the executive function of waking life ceases; and (3) Freud's “dream work” is reinterpreted as describing the predream storage transformation of perceptions and thought into the LTMS. One further conjecture is made: Memories are stored in the LTMS according to what is already in the LTMS. The observables of Freud's theory remain the same. The new theory is also consistent with recent experimental findings and suggests a partial basis for personality: the selection process of the storage transformation. The existence of a consciousness pointer is hypothesized to reflect dreams being limited to a single thread.

On 8-10 May 2003, the Mexican neuro-psychoanalysis group convened a scientific symposium in Guadalajara, Mexico, on the topic of “Brain: Emotion and Cognition,” organized by the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Guadalajara and the scientific commission of the Mexican Psychiatric Association. About 400 people came to the great event, because of interest in the interface between cognitive neuroscience, psychiatry, and psychoanalysis.

Professor Karl Pribram was our distinguished foreign guest, but there were many Mexican speakers presenting their scientific work. Among these was Dr. Carlos Rodríguez-Betancourt, Dr. Teresita Villaseñor-Cabrera, Dr. Claudia Castro-Delgadillo, Dr. Dante Medina, Dr. Fernando Moreno-Castillo, and Dr. Daniel Ojeda-Torres.

Professor Karl Pribram gave a lecture on “Freud in the Twenty-First Century.” The cognitive revolution linked with computational science brings a new approach to the old mind—brain problem. He proposes a holographic model, where neural mechanisms related to memory and learning play a role and the amygdala functions as the nodal point of the complex neuronal network controlling the instinctive behaviors that ensure the survival of the species.

Dr. Moreno-Castillo gave a talk on “The Frontier of Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience” and suggested that psychoanalytic thinking has been particularly valuable in recognizing the diversity and complexity of human mental experience, where factors of both a genetic and a social origin determine the mental representations of the world. The progress of cellular neurobiology can help to open new roads also within psychoanalysis.

There were also presentations by Dr. Rodríguez-Betancourt on “The Neurology of Nirvana,” Dr. Medina on “Neurodiscourse and Narrative,” and Dr. Castro-Delgadillo on “Language and Affectivity.”

With this scientific meeting we have taken our first step in constructing new bridges between psychoanalysis and neuroscience in Mexico.

Affect, Empathy, and Self-Awareness

Panskepp, J. (2003). At the interface of the affective, behavioural, and cognitive neurosciences: Decoding the emotional feelings of the brain.Brain and Cognition, 52: 4-14.

This paper is part of a wonderful special issue of Brain and Cognition, which I would highly recommend for those wanting to survey the diversity of opinion among modern neuroscientists on issues of emotion and affect. In this review, Panksepp sets out his views on the question of whether the traditional distinction between emotion and cognition still has heuristic value. For many readers the distinction appears obvious, but there have been many in modern cognitive neuroscience who hold that “the distinction between emotional and cognitive process was counterproductive” (p. 7). Given that the distinction is of central importance to many ideas within psychoanalysis, it is good to see Panksepp outlining the many compelling reasons that support this important dichotomy, such as the link between true emotion and valence/value, the cortical versus subcortical anatomical dissociation, the primacy of affective states in the young, and the preservation of emotional states even after extensive damage to cognitive systems. Panksepp is fighting a battle in which he lies in numerical minority, but in which the big guns of empirical neuroscience appear to support his argument. Given that his position on the importance of emotion in mental life is entirely congruent with central ideas in psychoanalysis, readers are strongly encouraged to read this paper, and related parts of the special issue, to keep abreast of these important issues.

Hamm, A. O., Weike, A. I., Schupp, H. T., Trieg, T., Dressel, A., & Kessler, C. (2003). Affective blindsight: Intact fear conditioning in a cortically blind patient.Brain, 126: 267-275.

We have known for several decades—since the early work of Weizkrantz—that some patients with lesions to the cortical visual system lack a conscious experience of vision but retain visual capabilities that are outside awareness: so called “blindsight.” We also know that these residual capabilities probably reflect the operation of intact subcortical systems for vision. However, previous work on blindsight has typically stressed the intact abilities of these patients on simple cognitive tasks such as location and movement detection. The study conducted by Hamm and coworkers extends our knowledge into the domain of emotion. It demonstrates that a patient with blindsight retains fear conditioning—the ability to know that a visual event will predict an aversive event (such as electric shock)—despite being subjectively blind. The paper represents an important vindication of the psychoanalytic claim that emotional consequences can be triggered without conscious awareness and the neuroscientific claim that subcortical systems mediate emotion (see the Panksepp paper reviewed above). However, as Hamm has recently acknowledged in a correspondence with Panksepp, Hamm et al. did not actually ask their patient how he felt during the various events in the task—so that the measure of emotion in the paper remains behavioral, and not as “affective” as the title suggests. Hamm has agreed to rectify this omission when next he tests the patient—and we all look forward to the day when neuroscientists working on emotion will think of asking their patients how they feel, without having to be prompted.

[[RunningHead]]

Commentary on “On the Nature of Repressed Contents”

Are Unconscious Mental States Really Neurophysiological Dispositions? Why Searle's Model of the Unconscious Won't Do

David Smith

David Smith

Portland, Maine

David Smith   Director, New England Institute for Cognitive Science and Evolutionary Psychology, Portland, Maine, U.S.A.

“Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.”

George Santayana

Philosophy of mind and cognitive science provide important concepts and tools for making sense of the architecture of mind. One of the most prominent contributors to the debates in this arena is the philosopher John Searle. Vesa Talvitie and Juhani Ihanus have taken the very useful step of exploring how Searle's approach might clarify our conception of the unconscious. Although I do not share their evaluation of Searle, I applaud their effort.

I shall first explore the historical background of the debate that Searle has revived (a position very much like the one that he espouses was widely held in the nineteenth century) and then go on to present Searle's theory and some objections to it, culminating in an argument against the dispositionalist position derived from the work of Sigmund Freud. Finally, I shall comment on some reservations expressed by Talvitie and Ihanus about my interpretation of the strength of this argument.

Historical Background

In order to come to grips with the debate about the nature of unconscious mental states, one must begin in the seventeenth century, when René Descartes propounded his highly influential model of the mind. The Cartesian platform was built from three planks, each resting upon the previous one, namely:

Minds and bodies are different kinds of thing, which interact with one another. Bodies are material things, operating on mechanical principles, whereas minds are nonmaterial things.

Minds are entirely conscious. They can neither be mistaken about nor ignorant of their own contents.

Introspection provides a true account of mental contents.

Over the centuries, aspects of the model were modified (most notable, the notoriously problematic claim that body and mind interact), but the fundamental notion that mind is a nonphysical and entirely conscious entity remained the dominant psychological perspective until at least the early decades of the twentieth century.

Vesa Talvitie and Juhani Ihanus

Juhani Ihanus

Juhani Ihanus  

What is it Like to be Unconsciously Mental?

In our target article we aimed to transform philosophical—we think mainly useless—speculations concerning the mental nature of the unconscious into scientific or neurophysiological issues. When looking at the comments, it becomes evident that we have failed completely: philosophical issues have a prominent role in the comments of the reviewers. Moreover, none of the reviewers sees the basic line of thought of our article to be fruitful when the dilemma between the psychoanalytic and the cognitive unconscious is attempted to be resolved.

However, every reviewer thinks the topic to be important—this is not a surprise, because we are dealing with the “cornerstone” of psychoanalysis. Sharing this idea, and being glad to have an opportunity to study this topic together with the reviewers, we will still try to argue in favor of our view.

“Mental,” facts, and explanations

“Mental” is a tricky term. It is (together with “psychic”) probably the most common psychological term, but there is no standard definition for it. For us (and for Searle and many others, too), the term mental is inescapably tied to the unique characteristics of consciousness: emotions, affects, and the feeling of what it is like to possess a certain idea. However, it is often used in a very general sense to refer to processes that occur, or structures that exist, in the mind/brain (of humans). Only few researchers—in addition to psychoanalytic ones, or, for example, the HOT-theorists (see Gennaro, 1996, pp. 103-120)—have reasons to debate whether unconscious matters are mental or not.

When pondering if A has a property of B or not, we usually know what B is, and how it may appear to us. We know how to find out if a certain matter is, for example, wet or radioactive. In the present topic, however, the foundations are quite different. In the domain of psychoanalysis, we are accustomed to thinking that the unconscious is mental, but it has never been clear what this means. Consequently, in the present discussion there is an emphasis on trying to find a suitable definition for the term mental.

James Deutsch

James Deutsch

email: j.deutsch@utoronto.ca

James Deutsch  

The Toronto group continues to focus on traumatic and depressive syndromes, applying psychoanalytic and neuroscientific knowledge with the goal of an integrated understanding of the patient. The past few meetings have involved presentations by members of the group focusing on qualitative research, anthropology, and clinical work.

Wendy Tevins presented on “Enigmatic Illness and the Wounded Self: A Qualitative Study of Women with Fibromyalgia and Chronic Fatigue Syndrome.” The effect of economic and social factors in a situation of prolonged stress and trauma threatens the maintenance of self-coherence and meaning. Descriptive diagnostic categories, such as the DSM, do not do justice to the psychological or putative biological concomitants. Multiple etiologies are suggested, including viral infection, reduction of signal to noise, problems with prefrontal gating, loss of useful function, and “falling out of culture.” The life-history approach underlined the alienation and devastating loss. Several case studies were presented. Similarities to multi-infarct dementia and to shamanism, among other phenomena, were noted. It was also commented that there is a lack of in-depth psychoanalytic literature in this area.

Paul Antze presented “An Anthropological Perspective on Multiple Personality Disorder/DID.” He had been asked to lead a group of patients with these diagnoses and had brought his anthropological skills to addressing the arbitrary divisions among biological, social, and cultural descriptive categories. Various cultures were contrasted in terms of the degree of individuality and idioms of distress and illness. Ranges between emotional outburst and extremes of self-control as the norm were contrasted with the special status (including suffering) of the person who dissociates. Diagnostic trends were traced in terms of economic, legal, and political forces.

The group consisted of high-functioning women with careers, many of them the mothers of small children. An integrated understanding was built of the components of fantasy, psychic reality, construction of the world through idioms, the notion of co-conscious-ness, and various metaphors of language such as “splitting migraine,” identification, introjection, and shifting cathexis.

There are at present three study groups working in Stockholm and one in Malmö-Lund in the south of Sweden. During the autumn term of 2002, after finishing reading Sexing the Brain by Leslie Rogers, the Body- Mind Study Group revisited Clinical Studies in Neuro-Psychoanalysis by Karen Kaplan-Solms and Mark Solms, to which we had earlier devoted much time. E. Gori  

The group is carrying on its work in a number of psychoanalysis centers in various towns and cities. These groups meet every three months to exchange information regarding their research areas. We held a workshop both at the EPF Congress in Prague, 2002, and at the SPI National Congress in Trieste, 2002, during which relations between recent scientific discoveries in the field of neuroscience and memory structuring, seen from the psychoanalytic point of view, were explored. The neurobiologist who also took part reported on mnemonic classifications put forward by neuroscientists. The general aim was to see which aspects of memory described in terms of psychoanalytic development might (or might not) be confirmed by neurobiological research. The following are some abstracts of the subjects presented:

E. C. Gori: “Primary Memory: Between Psychoanalytic Setting and Neurobiology.” Usually the names are different, but the functions described are very similar. It has also been noted that neurobiologists, following Kandel (1998, 1999), do not take into consideration the primal repression function proposed by Freud (1915a, 1915b, 1919, 1929, 1950 [1895]). Freud proposed that at the start of life drives and emotions do not cathect all thing-presentations and therefore they play no part in the construction of the id, which is the first locus in which cathected presentations are stored. Freud draws a distinction between primal repression and secondary repression (a function of the ego). Thus, the first function of the id is not repressive, since at this point there is no ego: the first memories are actively placed in the body. We are also considering the function of words and affects in the construction of memory and whether neuroscience might improve the therapeutic relationship (transference-countertransference) or whether we must expect further developments in the field of neurobiology. Starting out from the clinical encounter, we have begun studying the way neurobiological sciences deal with defenses—that is, the question of whether a distinction is made between primal defenses (denial, rejection, etc.) and secondary defenses (secondary repression, process of identification, etc.) (Winnicott, 1951, 1965).

New York/Boston/Dordrecht/London/Moscow: Kluwer Academic/Plenum Publishers, 2001. ISBN: 0-306-46494-2, 184 pp., $49.50.

Alexandre Métraux

Alexandre Métraux

Quincy, MA 02169
(email: drwatt@brahmacom.com)

email: ametraux@aol.com

Alexandre Métraux  

This book is about the life and work of Alexander Luria, a prominent figure in the history of twentieth-century neuropsychology and a person who, according to most of his students and friends, had multiple talents as a researcher, theorist, teacher, and prolific writer. But this “scientific biography” is neither the first contribution of its kind, nor is it apt to significantly further the understanding of Luria's life and work.

There is no doubt that Luria has already received more than just a modest amount of attention from historically minded authors and readers. The point at stake, therefore, ultimately ought to be whether, given that Luria has received considerable attention, Evgenia Homskaya's book meets the criteria a monograph of this sort is usually expected to meet.

In the introductory chapter the author characterizes her teacher and friend as an “exceptional scientist as well as an extraordinary person,” as a man who “belonged to that exclusive category of scientists who have a great number of students and followers during their lifetime,” as someone who was able “to assimilate into psychology the ideas of different adjacent disciplines, such as neurology, physiology, anatomy, biology, and others,” as an “outstanding researcher,” as someone (but here I interrupt the nearly unending list of attributes Ms Homskaya ascribes to the hero of her monograph) whose “most attractive characteristic … was his benevolence” (all quotes are taken from pp. 1-3 of the book under review). Luria was, indeed, a socially visible and exceptionally productive researcher. Yet, one might raise the question as to whether a biographer's admiration for—and yearlong collaboration with—the person to be analytically portrayed is by itself a sufficient condition for an informative historical study, especially if the outcome of this study seeks to convey more than the author's private recollections.

Luria published two self-portraits: in 1974 a short self-presentation in volume IV (pp. 253-292) of A History of Psychology in Autobiography (edited by G. Lindzey), and in 1979 the book-length The Making of Mind. A Personal Account of Soviet Psychology (edited by Michael and Sheila Cole). These self-portraits were followed in 1994 by the Russian publication Moy Otets A. R. Luriya [My Father A. R. Luria] by Elena Luria, the daughter's personal account, which did not even aim to hide the fact that it was drawn from a lovingly partisan view on Alexander Romanovich. But this latter book contained valuable documents stemming from the large family archive. Thus, Homskaya's monograph turns out to be the fourth in a series of autobiographical and heterobiographical publications dealing nearly exclusively with Luria's life and work. It also reveals itself to be an unsatisfying contribution to the biographical literature. Indeed, it does not present new archival documents, nor does it outline an alternative, original, empirically well-grounded approach to its subject.

Our group is now a society. This was the best way we found of encouraging more professionals to get engaged in what has been studied around the world related to neuro-psychoanalysis. Professionals and students of brain-mind science can take part in group studies or receive news about the progress in neuropsychoanalysis. The society will also organize meetings. We are looking forward with enthusiasm to our first meeting, which will take place on 29-30 September 2003, with Mark Solms as invited speaker.

During the half-year preceding the September meeting some of the founding members of the SSBNP will prepare the community on mental health in Brazil by giving seminars on Solms's work.

For more than a year, several members of the SSBNP (Karla Nyland, Cleon Cerezer, Andre Goettens Bastos, Angela Piva, Beatriz Zimerman, Claudia Albuquerque Ramos, Elizabeth M. da Silva Vieira, and Maria Sonia Goergen) have been working together on a research project on neurological patients, where several perspectives have been applied: psychoanalytic treatment, speech therapy, neurological follow up, and pharmacological treatment.

During the first two months not only did some patients desert the study, but also some psychotherapists. It took some time for the therapists to understand and accept that this was an interdisciplinary work and that all aspects were important, the main objective being to help the patients to improve functions lost or not yet achieved.

A special characteristic of this group is that all the patients are children. Here are some short notes from the patients’ material:

“Fernando” was a healthy 10-year-old boy when he suffered a severe head injury in a car accident. He also lost his father and other close relatives in the accident. He was in a coma for months and after regaining consciousness was found to have a left hemiplegia. He had bad control of his social behavior and language, being crude and impolite as well as manifesting slurred speech. He is improving well, but there is still a long way to go.

James Deutsch  

The Toronto group has been focusing on traumatic and depressive syndromes and on applying psychoanalytic knowledge toward the goal of an integrated understanding of the suffering person. To this end, we have been looking at what is available from brain imaging and, at the same time, at what is useful or problematic in current psychoanalytic dialogue.

Drs. Clare Pain and Ruth Lanius gave a presentation on trauma and dissociation theory and imaging. Early writers hypothesized thoughts and memories, preserved in the unconscious, as being “pushed away” but exerting pressure. While life is a continuum, the experience of continuity may be the exception rather than the rule. Animal responses to danger situations are different from human responses. In some individuals, dissociative phenomena in trauma may represent the outcome of structural states rather than defensive processes—that is, pathological and “normal” dissociation may be qualitatively distinct. The developmental stage of the traumatic occurrence(s)—especially with regard to verbalization—as well as present-day physiological state may have a bearing on the potential for “archeological” investigation of memories.

Dr. Lanius presented functional MRI investigations of the neural correlates of recalling traumatic memories. Her work—partly reported in Lanius et al., Biol. Psychiatry, 52 (15 Aug. 2002/no. 4): 305-311 and in Lanius et al., Biol. Psychiatry, 53 (1 Feb. 2003/no. 3): 204-210—focused on, among others, victims of mo-tor-vehicle accidents hearing prepared narrative scripts of their experiences while being scanned. In the clinical study of the acute posttraumatic state, a man who actively dealt with an accident demonstrated a richer activation pattern, which contrasted with that of his wife, who had frozen during the accident, and who had had a difficult early history. The results suggested that the diagnostic subcategories of hyperarousal and hypoarousal should be considered for future studies. PTSD subjects showed significantly less activation of the thalamus and the anterior cingulate gyrus (area 32) than did trauma-exposed controls. The thalamus, described as the sensory gateway having a key role in “core consciousness,” was also less active in patients with hyperarousal at the time of imaging. Visual cortex was more active. There was discussion of the functional MRI findings in light of literature with PET, which may be less helpful with subcortical structures. There were also suggestions for refining study protocols to match clinically useful paradigms more closely.

David D. Olds's “Affect as a Sign System”

Maxine Sheets-Johnstone

Maxine Sheets-Johnstone

Yachats, Oregon

Maxine Sheets-Johnstone   Department of Philosophy, University of Oregon, Eugene, Oreg., U.S.A.

Toward a Semiotic Reconstruction

Dr. David Olds's paper1 on the possible application of a Peircean semiotics to psychoanalysis is particularly stimulating and explorative in its concluding two subsections. In these pages, Dr. Olds discusses three aspects of affect and their possible dissociations, and the import of the symbolization of affect. His discussions bring to the fore in explicit ways the possible value of a semiotic modeling of affect and, in the process, exemplify concretely the possible relevance of a semiotic point of view to psychoanalytic practice. I would like to suggest a salutary move: a semiotic reconstruction of his Peircean application that begins with these two subsections. In this reconstructed paper, the move would be from a descriptive analysis of the clinical semiotics operative in psychoanalytic practice to possible neurological–physiological semiotic correlates. The critical comments that follow are geared to that reconstructive effort and intended to be read as such—that is, as positive in their aim.

I

As Olds intimates in speaking of “the possibility of a unified theory of mind and brain” (p. 82), and of the way a semiotic model “approaches” the question of “the necessary dualism in a world where there are irreducible dichotomies such as those between the animate and the inanimate, and between the mind and the brain,” the appeal of Peirce's semiotics lies in the fact that it is applicable across dichotomies (and academic divisions). Because it is basically a metaphysical system, it ostensibly lets one pass effortlessly from one level of reality to another— that is, from experience to physiology to brains … and back. In this sense, it is indeed a heuristic, precisely as Olds views it in the context of his study, and precisely as he intimates when he states that “we follow the flow of information; we attend to patterns and structures that are transformed as information travels in living organisms” (p. 83). The end result, however, is less than heuristic. The free passage from brains to intact living organisms and from intact living organisms to brains, with substantive diversions along the way into physiology, has its costs in both credibility and clarity. One might say that the semiotic application covers more ground than it can properly manage and, in covering so much ground, summarily brushes aside obstacles in its path. Most prominent with respect to the former is the problem of mixed levels of discourse; most prominent with respect to the latter is the nettlesome problem of meaning as distinct from information. The costs are not necessarily fatal to a heuristic application of a Peircean semiotics, but they surely demand responsible and full settlement. In what follows, I shall spell out conceptual muddles and omissions and then mention incidental but related difficulties. In the process, I hope to bring to the fore two major points: the surprising persistence of William James's psychology of emotions, and the fact that, whether by way of neurology or semiotics, language cannot solve the mind–brain problem.

During this past year our research has advanced along two lines: (1) further exploring the nature of unconscious processes, and (2) providing an experimental basis for the theory of primary-and secondary-process mentation. Michel Silberfeld   Assistant Professor, Department of Psychiatry, Joint Centre for Bioethics, University of Toronto; President, Toronto Psychoanalytic Society; Coordinator, Competency Clinic, Baycrest Centre for Geriatric Care, North York, Ontario, Canada

This paper presents a clinical psychoanalytic examination of the location of meaning of the symptoms in patients with reduplicative paramnesia. The examination is set up first by a consideration of the countertransference problem—of awareness in another—to prepare for the views on the cases of reduplicative paramnesia. The psychoanalytic viewpoint is then contrasted with the psychiatric and neuropsychological perspectives. These differences are used to demonstrate a psychoanalytic standpoint in the debates about the location of meaning. Some conclusions are also drawn about the limits of empathy, the charitable requirements for interpretation, and when interpretation is likely to be an effective intervention.

A long and increasingly articulate line of behavioral researchers, therapists, and psychoanalysts has been bitten by the bug of nonlinear dynamic systems theory, better known since James Gleick (1987) as the new science of “Chaos” (cf. Chamberlain & Butz, 1998; Mandell & Selz, 1995; Moran, 1991; Robertson & Combs, 1995; Spruiell, 1993; Thelen & Smith, 1994). The reason is clear. Until the advent of chaos theory, there was no compelling way to mathematically simulate weather patterns, economic shifts, species evolution, neural network formation, or, last but not least, the intricacies of human intra- and interaction. Joining these other pioneers, Palombo has bravely left the safety net of traditional psychoanalytic theory and thoroughly immersed himself in one of the most fascinating offshoots of nonlinear exploration: the study of complex adaptive systems (i.e., complexity theory). With the help of one of its founders, Stuart Kauffman, Palombo has clearly studied more than just the basics of this complicated discipline. Along the way, he has also learned an impressive amount about the other first cousins of nonlinearity: coevolution, connectionism (neural networks), and game theory. Lastly, in order to integrate the role of interpretation in psychoanalysis, Palombo mustered the work of several prominent linguistic researchers.

The book he has written unwittingly affords the reader direct experience of one of its main underlying principles: that the maximal opportunity for psychotherapeutic change occurs “at the edge of chaos.” Each chapter pulls the reader away from various conventional ideas of psychoanalysis in order to provide a new perspective garnered from this potpourri of nonlinear viewpoints. However, even when one has managed, with a lot of close reading, a new anchor in one of the complicated models Palombo presents, one's footing is soon dislodged by the centrifugal force of yet another intricate concept. This taut sense of imbalance derives mainly from the vast span of knowledge that Palombo covers. However, there is also a sense that the author has missed certain opportunities to hone down, clarify, and integrate the dense material that he is presenting. The list of chapter headings will convey the magnitude of his sweep: (1) “The Evolutionary Process,” (2) “A Sampling of the Psychoanalytic Process,” (3) “Metabiology,” (4) “Complex Adaptive Systems,” (5) “Networks and Connections in the Brain,” (6) “The Edge of Chaos in the Therapeutic Process,” (7) “Coevolution in Coupled Systems: The Therapeutic Relationship,” (8) “Dreaming, Self-Or-ganization, and the Therapeutic Process,” (9) “The Mutative Interpretation,” (10) “The Beginning of an Analysis: A Case Illustration,” (11) “Conclusion.

Spinoza's Monism and the Idea of the Body

A reply to Heidi Ravven

Antonio Damasio

Antonio Damasio

Antonio Damasio  

I very much enjoyed reading Heidi Ravven's essay, to which I turned as the deadline for delivery of these replies approached. It is a beautifully written and deeply engaging piece of philosophy. I look forward to replying to it at length, in person and in writing, at a later date. For the time being, however, I have the following to say.

Looking for Spinoza was written in continuity with Feeling of What Happens, not quite in the same breath but certainly as an extension of the same set of facts and interpretations. Looking for Spinoza is neither a comprehensive review nor a synthesis. It is, rather, a sidestep meant to allow me some detailing of new information on the neurobiology of feeling and some space to reflect on Spinoza the thinker and the person. My notions of body, mind, self, emotion, and feeling did not change from one work to the other, and only the detail of the neural account of those phenomena evolved. Ravven states, quite correctly, that in Feeling of What Happens, “Damasio locates the origin of value as emerging from what he calls … the perspective of the body. That phrase, in my view, admirably captures Spinoza's understanding as well. In [Feeling of What Happens], Damasio is adamant about locating the origin of value in our organismic urge for homeostasis and, by extension, in the external objects and situations that promote it.” This is precisely the idea that I still hold and discuss in Looking for Spinoza.

Heidi Ravven suggests that my Spinozist position has been “attenuated to some extent” in the latest book. She says that in Looking for Spinoza I introduce “a strong dualism, absent from his previous book,” between emotions and feelings, a “dualism” that seems to modify my theoretical account of the emotions and of the origin of ethics. Moreover, she suggests that this “dualism” produces a “hiatus between the subcortical and the cortical.” I entirely disagree with this characterization of my thinking. Let me explain why.

First, the distinction between emotion and feeling, which I clearly articulate as a research strategy, has been present in all of my articles and books for over a decade. Feeling of What Happens repeatedly honors that distinction. In Looking for Spinoza I state clearly, at the outset and at the end of Chapter 3, that in practical terms emotion and feeling operate together, as affect, and that my distinction is an investigative ploy meant to uncover what lies beneath affect.

Commentary on “Understanding Addictive Vulnerability”

Val Morrison MA PHD C. Psychol.

Val Morrison

Val Morrison   University of Wales Bangor, U.K.

Furthering the Sociocognitive Explanation of Addiction

While exploring Khantzian's well-presented case as to why people become addicted, I became uncomfortable with the inference that all who become addicted use their drug(s) of choice to adapt to inner conflicts, psychopathology, or emotional pain or to control deficits in emotional regulation. The suggestion is of drug use as responding to a “drive” or compulsion outside the person's ultimate control— and this suggestion fails to square with a large segment of the literature on the topic of addiction. What of the more hedonically motivated goals of “having fun” and “rebellion”? These are strong and common motives for use (e.g., Jessor & Jessor, 1977), and while some might claim that they represent forms of psychopathology, they could only do so by pushing the boundaries of “pathology” to extraordinary limits. In addition, a focus on motivational theories of addiction takes us soon into the area of decision making (Sutton, 1987; West, 1989) and raises the question of social or subcultural norms, availability, expectancies, peer pressure, and reinforcement as influences upon our choices (Bandura, 1971, 1986; Orford, 1985). I feel these warrant more attention than the psychodynamic perspective allows.

There are many reasons to suggest that drug use may be maintained, not by physiological benefit and the removal of withdrawals (in part, addiction theory), nor by intrapersonal gain or self-medication (e.g., enhanced self-confidence, reduced anxiety), but by reinforcing friends and situations (sociallearning theory), achievement of self-selected goals (reinforcement), or pursuit of goals and the individual's motivational structure (e.g., Cox & Klinger, 2002). For example, Mischel (1977) notes that the interaction between personal disposition and the environment accounts for more variance in behavior than does either factor alone, or both together. Behavior is not caused only by either inner forces or external influences, but by an interaction between the two that varies depending on the individuals cognitions, appraisals, and expectancies. Thus, drug use can become an “occupation” that gives the person a sense of purpose and a series of tasks to do and goals (e.g., of procurement of drugs) to achieve, which in itself can be reinforcing. It has been repeatedly shown that young people's chronic drug use is commonly associated with a lack of “direction” in life, and perhaps that drug use and the associated rituals fill that gap at a given stage in an individual's life (e.g., Morrison, 1993; Newcomb & Harlow, 1986). For this reason, interventions are unlikely to succeed unless the availability and support of drug use changes locally, nationally, and internationally (Crowley, 1988) and unless alternative lifestyle directions or goal pursuits are identified and worked toward (e.g., Cox & Klinger, 1990, 2002).

Based on evidence for brain affective systems, parceled into six distinct groups (Panksepp, 1998a), it was hypothesized that a great deal of personality variability would be related to strengths and weaknesses found in these six systems. If supported, this hypothesis would provide further evidence for the physiological bases of personality. Personality scales, modeled after the Spielberger State-Trait Personality Inventory (STPI), were constructed to estimate self-reported feedback concerning the putative influences of these six neurally based networks, which are labeled PLAY, SEEK, CARE, FEAR, ANGER, and SADNESS systems, along with a Spirituality scale and various filler questions. Subjects completed these Affective Neuroscience Personality Scales (ANPS) as well as a Five-Factor Model (FFM) scale. Data revealed various strong relationship between the APNS and the FFM scales. Implications for psychometric theory, the relationships between affect and personality, as well as the physiological bases of personality are discussed.

Clifford Yorke

Clifford Yorke

Clifford Yorke   Hon. Consultant Psychiatrist, Anna Freud Centre, London

Some Reflections on Addiction

The target paper

I read Professor Khantzian's target paper with some disappointment, and I was unhappy when I was asked to be a discussant.

His observations cover a great deal of ground but do not, to my mind, make an appropriate basis for an exchange of views between psychoanalysts and neuroscientists on the vexing question of addiction. Indeed, his “psychodynamic perspective” seems to minimize some crucial psychoanalytic concepts. Unconscious mental functioning receives scant, if any, attention, outside the following sentence:

Contemporary psychodynamic theory in application to SUDs paralleled developments in modern psychoanalytic thinking by laying less emphasis on drives and unconscious conflicts, but placing greater emphasis on appreciating the importance of affects, on the development of ego and self structures, and on the quality of and capacity for relationships and connection to others.

“Less emphasis” could well be read as “little emphasis” without doing any disservice to the general purport of the text. (SUDS—“substance-use disorders”—seems the preferred term to drug addiction nowadays, but seems to me insufficiently explicit.)

The point about affects calls for immediate comment. Freud's views on affects have been effectively and cogently discussed in this Journal by Solms and Nersessian (1999); also, the point that, without a concept of drives, there is no psychoanalytic concept of either thought or affect has been emphasized by others, including the writer (Yorke, 1999a, 1999b). For Freud, a drive can only be known through its mental representatives, of which the quantitative aspects are perceived as affects (the qualitative ones are thoughts). In psychoanalytic thinking there can be no affects without drives, about which Khantzian borders on the dismissive. And what is meant by “self structures”? If Khantzian means self-representations, these are conceived, psychoanalytically, as complex mental organizations, conscious and unconscious, to which all parts of the personality make contributions—a statement equally true of object representations. The latter are not mentioned in spite of their ready interaction with, and reciprocal influence upon, self-representations. Whatever Khantzian's “psychodynamic theory” is, it is clearly not based on psychoanalytic thinking, modern or otherwise.

The Freudian Theory of Psychic Structuring from an Evolutionary Perspective

Victor Andrade MD

Victor Andrade

Av. Princesa Isabel, 150/Gr. 1201, Copacabana, 22011-010 Rio de Janeiro—RJ, Brazil.
(email: victormanoel@alternex.com.br)

Victor Andrade   Member of the Rio de Janeiro Psychoanalytical Society, Brazil.

Freud regarded affect as the outcome of secretory or vasomotor discharge inside the body. This paper describes the genesis and development of the psyche in view of this bodily characteristic of the affects, based on the obscure Freudian concept of affective structure. This notion is seen here as the memory trace of the first experiences of pleasure and unpleasure, which constitute the germinal core of the mind. “The exigencies of life” bring about a process by which automatic regulation by the pleasure principle is replaced by thought, at which point ideational structures become superimposed over affective structures. The evolution from affective to ideational structures is described, as well as the way in which these latter acquire psychic quality (consciousness) through memory residues of speech. The role of the object in structuring affective experiences is underscored, as it is this role that makes transference the pillar of support for the psychoanalytic process. Affect and thought are seen as inextricable, a fact that, besides reinforcing Freud's conviction that psychoanalysis is a natural science, gives Freudian metapsychology sufficient range to make it a theoretical support for the clinical advances being made by different currents today and to aid in arriving at a desired common ground.

By the end of 2003, six years will have passed since the first Swedish group started on its adventure to study the newly opened arena within psychoanalysis of body–mind and consciousness studies. In 2004 we hope to be able to evaluate and draw some conclusions from this experience. We will then be happy to report our insights in this forum; but until then the groups will continue their work as related below.

The original Body–Mind Study Group turned, at the beginning of 2003, to a semiotic study of the old nature/culture questions, ranging from the biochemical level within cell structures (mitochondria, etc.) to animal and human behavior. We are using Jesper Hoffmeyer's book Life-Signs: The Natural History of Meaning as our guide (Hoffmeyer is professor of molecular biochemistry in Copenhagen). The group is chaired by Iréne Matthis.

During the spring term of 2003, the nine members of the Study Group on the Philosophy of Psychology, guided by the philosopher Lars-Göran Johansson, read and discussed Ian Hacking's Social Construction of What? Next on our agenda, for the start of the autumn term, is the JAPA 47/2 paper by Charles Hanly, “On Subjectivity and Objectivity.”

At the full-day seminar the method of doing a pathobiography, as it is used at the Weizsäcker Institute in Buenos Aires, was presented. To illustrate the method, a clinical case of severe hemorrhoid suffering, investigated at the Weizsäcker Institute, was presented.

Transparent Feelings

A Reply to Jaak Panksepp and Douglas Watt

Antonio Damasio

Antonio Damasio

Antonio Damasio  

I must begin by thanking Jaak Panksepp and Douglas Watt (P & W) for the attention they have given my recent book and the effort they have made to deal with its substance. In their text they indicate that they share many of my views and that they have opted to focus their appraisal on areas of disagreement. That is where I will focus my reply as well.

The issues raised by P & W can be divided into two groups: one group concerns several misunderstandings of my positions; another concerns genuine differences of point of view. I will address the misunderstandings first.

P & W profess admiration for my last book, The Feeling of What Happens, especially in regard to a number of issues over which, after reading of Looking for Spinoza, they now disagree with me. Considering that I have not changed my views on any of those issues, it is reasonable to wonder what could possibly have caused this misunderstanding. Out of courtesy and modesty, perhaps I should simply take the blame and say that it is all my fault, that I simply should have made my writing more clear so that P & W would not be so confused. Unfortunately, it is not so easy. I have no doubt I could have made myself more clear, but perhaps some of the misunderstandings come from reading the material with an attitude that I can only describe as militant. That attitude, which I have previously encountered in the presentations of one of the reviewers, Jaak Panksepp, tends to interfere with a fair appraisal of ideas. It pertains to three tenets:

That what counts in the neuroscience of emotions and feelings are processes that occur subcortically, especially in the brainstem, and even more especially in the periaqueductal gray.

That animals in general and mammals for certain have feelings and consciousness as much as humans do.

That feelings are inseparable from emotions and share their motor-action nature.

Panksepp's views of research on emotion are filtered through these three tenets, and only work that passes the litmus test of adherence to these ideas is given the seal of approval. For example, work that focuses on cortical structures or on the amygdala is derided as “cortico-centric” and “amygdalo-centric”; the absence of an unequivocal proclamation that animals are conscious and feeling beings triggers a lament for any findings obtained without the upfront acknowledgment of that idea; and attempts to separate the physiology of emotion and feeling meets with two objections: first, that the strategy opens the way to denying feelings to animals; second, that it turns feelings into passive states—that is, when feelings are uncoupled from all the action intrinsic to emotion, they become limp and ineffectual phenomena. Through and through, P & W fault me, in my recent book, for a lack of unequivocal obeisance to these tenets, and although they leave open the possibility that they misunderstood me, they write largely as if they did not.

Understanding Addictive Vulnerability

An Evolving Psychodynamic Perspective

E. Khantzian MD

E. Khantzian

10-12 Phoenix Row, Haverhill, MA 01832, U.S.A.
email: drejk17@aol.com

E. Khantzian   Harvard Medical School, Boston, Mass.; Tewksbury Hospital, Tewksbury, Mass., U.S.A.

In contrast to early psychoanalytic theory, which stressed pleasurable/aggressive drives and the symbolic meaning of drugs to explain their appeal, a modern psychodynamic perspective of substance-use disorders (SUDs) places greater emphasis on intolerable painful or confusing affects that make addictive drugs compelling. A psychotherapeutic relationship rooted in a psychodynamic approach yields valuable data on the nature of a person's distress and deficits in psychological (ego/self) structures that predispose individuals to addiction. An evolving psychodynamic perspective, spanning 30 years, is presented wherein addictions have been considered as (1) a special adaptation, (2) an attempt to self-medicate painful or confusing emotions, (3) an overarching problem in self-regulation, and finally (4) a reflection of disorder in personality organization. This evolving perspective more likely than not should and does complement and resonate with other perspectives. A modern psychodynamic perspective of SUDs adds an important dimension to unraveling the biopsychosocial equation involved in understanding addictive vulnerability.

Jaak Panksepp  

“The Ego is First and Foremost a Body Ego”

Unraveling the innate affective values of the human brain might be the most captivating, and conceptually critical, aspect of the entire mind sciences. In trying to understand the neural foundations for emotional behaviors and emotional experience, one is truly seeking to map out the neural ground of our being. We have seen a critical renaissance in affective neuroscience in the last tn years, as emotion has become increasingly the focus of empirical work, and a subject for major works by leading investigators, one of those leading the way being Antonio Damasio. In this—his third—major contribution to the ongoing discussion of how emotional valuing is organized in the human brain, Antonio Damasio sails gracefully over this increasingly large body of work. As discussions of our emotional nature are again penetrating deeply into the humanities (e.g., McLemee, 2003), many recognize that a common denominator for bringing clarity to this topic is a confrontation with the evolved (inherited) nature of our emotional apparatus which does not neglect nature–nurture interactions and the complex and diverse, socially constructed cultural manifestations of our feelings.

In the present offering, Damasio seeks to captivate those outside the mind sciences, as he continues to argue for the importance of certain brain and body processes in the generation of the many emotional feelings that characterize the pains and satisfactions of individual lives. Considering the degree to which this book reflects Damasio's meditation on a topic of great personal interest to him, and no less to us, rather than a fully balanced account of the scientific state of the field, we would note that our applause is directed more toward the former and our criticisms at the relative paucity of the latter. Damasio's reversion to what at least seems to us a more cortico-centric view of experienced emotions in the present book left us a bit saddened, for we had both found his impressive second book (The Feeling of What Happens, 1999b) to be a badly needed tonic and valuable corrective to the prevailing cortico-centric bias in many treatments of both emotion and consciousness (Panksepp, 2000b; Watt, 2000b).

Synthesizing Psychoanalytic and Biological Approaches to Trauma

Some Theoretical Proposals

José Saporta MD

José Saporta

53 Beverly Road, Newton Highlands, MA 02461, U.S.A
(email: JSaportajr@aol.com)

José Saporta   Center for Psychoanalytic Studies, Massachusetts General Hospital; Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute, Newton Highlands, Mass., U.S.A.

This paper offers some theoretical possibilities for synthesizing psychoanalytic and neurobiological approaches to understanding the effects of severe psychic trauma. The paper argues that biological and psychoanalytic perspectives can enrich and enhance each other in our attempt to understand and ameliorate the damaging consequences of trauma. The findings of biological researchers and the observations of psychoanalysts are integrated, as they apply to two functions that are damaged by trauma: the capacity for representation and the capacity for self-regulation. These capacities are interdependent and interactive. Disrupting either will affect the other. The combined result of this disruption can profoundly alter subjective experience. The paper discusses how helping patients to symbolize traumatic experiences, affect, and other mental states and helping patients regulate physiology and affect through nonverbal, affect-regulating interactions, and through the use of medication, lead to an improved capacity to symbolize, to experience meaning, and to relate and can lead to a subjective sense of increased strength.

Jaak Panksepp

Jaak Panksepp   Bowling Green State University, Bowling Green, Ohio, U.S.A.

Toward a Comprehensive Psychobiological Theory of Addictions

Professor Khantzian shares an emotion-regulation- centered depth-psychological perspective on addictive processes. Rather than critique his even-handed coverage, I would merely supplement his views with some current neuroscientific perspectives in the area. There is still a vast chasm between these approaches, and the needed bridges can only sustain commerce if there is substantive building from both sides with concrete empirical predictions that can be evaluated in laboratory and clinic. To some extent that has already happened, with the recognition by both sides that certain evolved psycho-neuro mechanisms of the brain, such as the mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine SEEKING pathways (ML/MC DAp), are essential in all kinds of appetitive urges, including ones related to most drugs of abuse (Berridge & Robinson, 1998; Ikemoto & Panksepp, 1999; Kelley, 1999; Koob & Le Moal, 2001; Wise, 1998). However, I will highlight certain problems that still impede progress across the modest bridges that we already have, in the hop that those fragile constructions can be replaced by sturdier ones.

The key issue for depth-psychology is how to utilize the emerging neuroscientific knowledge to hew new insights.

Douglas Watt  

There are a few truly landmark books in any science, a few works that virtually everyone in a field would unanimously agree are seminal, definitive, or a benchmark for the field. This is true even in neuroscience, where our fine-grained knowledge about the brain is expanding exponentially but where integration of knowledge and heuristic thinking about the brain inevitably lag behind the runaway overdose of exploding “facts” and findings.

It is particularly worth noting that there are also different kinds of seminal or landmark publications. First and most obviously, in the history of any science, it is the stunning empirical result that always garners the greatest attention—as it should. There are certainly several empirical findings that stand out in behavioral neuroscience, where an experimental or clinical result initiates a major paradigm shift or suddenly illuminates regions previously shrouded in ignorance and conceptual confusion. A famous example of this might be Dr. Alois Alzheimer's first clinical case description of a dementing disorder or the discovery that l-dopa helped to treat the symptoms of Parkinson's disease. There are also seminal monographs and books that aim to summarize many experimental or clinical findings by one investigator in the service of broad reformulations of basic theoretical assumptions. An example of this might be Luria's 1966 work, Higher Cortical Functions in Man, which was decades ahead of its time in unraveling the contributions of distributed cortical regions to cognitive and other higher brain functions in terms of Luria's functional network models. Other recent theoretical syntheses of this kind might certainly include Panksepp's Affective Neuroscience and Damasio's The Feeling of What Happens.

Calvin Yu

Calvin Yu

10 Wai Tsui Crescent, Braemar Hill Road, North Point, Hong Kong
email: calyu2000@hotmail.com

Calvin Yu  

This paper aims to resolve the contradictory findings between PET and human lesion methods with regard to the role of the frontal convexity in the functional architecture of dreaming, and to consider the neuroscientific justification for its presumed psychoanalytic counterpart—the dream censor—an ultimate parameter that is believed to be behind the scene in charge of the entire manifestation of dreaming in the Freudian model. In contrast to prevailing beliefs, the author asserts that the latest neurophysiological findings are not necessarily incompatible with the classical psychoanalytic notion of dream censorship, provided that misunderstanding and confusion surrounding the psychoanalytic concepts and localization matters are cleared. The paper concludes with a proposed neurodynamic model of dreaming (the neuro-structural model) on the basis of the reconcilement between classical Freudian dream theory and the contemporary neurophysiological findings enumerated in this series of papers.

A Neuro-Psychoanalytic Approach to Addiction

Psychodynamics or neuro-psychoanalysis?

Dr. Khantzian has done a masterful job of summarizing the psychodynamic literature on addiction. Khantzian states, “With some notable exception, it is surprising and unfortunate that since the 1970s there have been so few contributions from psychoanalysts addressing the dynamics of SUDs [substance use disorders].” If we add the statistics from McGinnis and Foege (1993) that drug addiction is responsible for 25% of all deaths in the United States (nicotine 19%, alcohol 5%, illegal drugs 1%) and obesity (food addiction) is responsible for another 14% of U.S. deaths, it becomes obvious that addiction is a pressing issue for psychoanalysis. Either many patients undergoing psychoanalytic therapy have active addictive issues and their therapists lack a good theoretical basis for understanding their issues and consequently ignore them, or these extremely common patients are being systematically turned away from psychoanalytic therapy because we lack a good theoretical basis for understanding their issues. I suspect both are true.

Since there is a major biological component to addiction, an important difficulty involved in using psychodynamics alone is that the biological nature of the addictive process becomes indistinct rather than standing clearly as one side of a dialectical process between psychology and biology. Neuropsychoanalysis dwells in the margin of psychoanalysis and biology from which Dr. Khantzian indicates synthetic models may be formulated.

I will use the definition of neuropsychoanalysis provided by Kaplan-Solms and Solms (2000, p. 62). Neuropsychoanalysis links mind and brain “to dissect the internal psychological structure of the various changes in personality, motivation, and complex emotion that occur following damage to different cerebral structures. Thereafter, the multiple underlying factors producing these symptoms and syndromes can be identified and each correlated with its anatomical ‘scene of action.
